Evidence boundary. This document uses the supplied material and NIST reference figures. No site-specific network configurations, inventories, protocols, ports, logs, process limits or approvals were provided. Therefore illustrations show relationships to document, not verified deployment. Site-specific fields remain to be confirmed. Candidate sources and connections must be validated before use.

1. What connections can an OT network have?

An OT network connects physical equipment, controllers, operators, engineering systems and selected business services. The table below identifies potential connections and evidence sources. It does not assert that any connection or source exists at your site.

Native logs, network observations and process measurements are different evidence types. Confirm availability with representative records before assigning detection coverage.

ConnectionPurpose and communicationPotential logging/evidence sourcesDetection opportunities and limitations
Sensors → PLC/process controllerMeasurements through electrical signals, remote I/O, fieldbus, or industrial EthernetController diagnostics; I/O module diagnostics; SCADA alarms; historian values and quality flagsMissing/stale measurements, unexpected value changes. Simple sensors may have no native security logs.
PLC/controller → valves, pumps, motors, drivesOutput commands; equipment feedback returns where providedController events; drive diagnostics; command audit records; historian command/feedback tagsUnexpected commands or command/feedback mismatch. A command does not prove physical movement.
HMI/control console ↔ controllerReads/subscriptions for display; operator requests and writesHMI audit trail; operator login records; controller logs; passive protocol recordsUnusual operator actions, unexpected source, supported write operations. Network evidence may lack user identity.
SCADA/control server ↔ PLC/RTUPolling, telemetry, alarms, supervisory commandsSCADA communication/event logs; protocol-driver logs; RTU diagnostics; network sensor recordsPolling loss, unexpected commands, new peers, communication errors.
Engineering workstation ↔ controllerDiagnostics, programming, configuration, upload/downloadEngineering-software audit; endpoint process events; project/change records; controller audit; protocol monitoringEngineering activity outside authorization; configuration changes. Application execution needs endpoint evidence.
Controller ↔ controllerEquipment coordination, interlocks, shared stateController communication diagnostics; passive industrial-protocol monitoring; relevant process tagsNew controller peers, unexpected exchanges, lost coordination. Some traffic remains entirely inside a cell.
Historian ↔ SCADA/OPC server/controllerRead/subscription or pushed collection of process valuesHistorian collector logs; OPC server audit/session logs; database audit; historian quality/timestampsCollection gaps, unexpected clients, unauthorized historical-data changes. Compression can hide brief changes.
Application/OPC client ↔ OPC serverAccess process objects and exchange valuesOPC application audit; session/security logs; certificate events; endpoint logs; supported network decodingNew clients, failed sessions, unauthorized operations. Encryption may prevent passive payload inspection.
OT historian/exporter ↔ DMZ reporting serviceReplicate selected production informationReplication logs; application/service-account logs; firewall sessions; database auditUnexpected replication destinations, failed transfers, unapproved data exchange.
Enterprise/MIS/ERP ↔ DMZ exchange serviceReporting, production schedules, approved business integrationERP/application audit; API/access logs; file-transfer logs; DMZ firewall logsUnapproved business-to-OT exchanges or access paths. Business integration may have flows in both directions.
Vendor/remote engineer → gateway → jump host → OT targetApproved remote support and engineering accessVPN/access gateway; MFA/identity provider; PAM/session recordings; jump-host logons; target audit; firewall logsUnapproved users, targets, windows, or bypass paths. Correlate identity with the target activity.
OT systems ↔ authentication servicesUser authentication and authorizationOT identity-server audit; workstation/server logons; application authentication logsFailed logins, unusual privileged access, account changes. Not every field device uses central identity.
OT hosts → time/name servicesClock synchronization and name resolutionDNS query logs; time-service health/offset records; configuration audit; network recordsUnexpected DNS destinations, time drift, infrastructure changes. Not every time request is logged.
OT systems ↔ backup/update servicesBackups, approved software transfer, restorationBackup job logs; repository access; update-management records; endpoint/file-integrity eventsUnexpected restores, backup failure, unauthorized package deployment.
Network/security devices → collector/SIEMExport events, alerts, and health informationFirewall/router/switch logs; IDS records; collector health; ingestion/parser recordsTelemetry loss, configuration changes, blocked connections, visibility degradation.
SCADA control centre ↔ remote stationsTelemetry and commands over WAN, cellular, or radioSCADA communication logs; RTU/controller diagnostics; WAN/VPN/firewall records; modem/radio diagnosticsUnexpected remote endpoints, link failures, unusual commands. IP sensors alone may not observe serial-radio traffic.
Primary ↔ backup/regional control centreReplication, redundancy, coordination, failoverControl-server redundancy logs; replication logs; authentication records; WAN/firewall logsUnexpected failover, replication loss, unauthorized secondary access. Confirm the actual control-authority model.
IIoT devices → edge gateway → platformTelemetry publishing, analytics, potentially device commandsGateway logs; MQTT broker or API audit where used; platform identity logs; device-management recordsNew publishers/subscribers, unexpected command channels, gateway configuration changes.
Wireless devices ↔ industrial access pointMobile HMI, sensors, maintenance connectivityAP/controller logs; wireless authentication; gateway records; endpoint logsUnknown clients, configuration changes, unexpected wireless access.
BPCS ↔ SIS, where explicitly engineeredSelected measurements, status, or other approved interfacesSafety-system diagnostics/audit; engineering records; interface logs; available process historyUnexpected engineering changes or interface loss. Separate controllers do not establish independent protection.

Maintain a status for each row: verified present / verified absent / unknown, followed by operational owner, evidence reference and validation date. Never convert “unknown” to “not present.”

Use the supplied NIST figures as architecture options, selected according to the real installation. Start from the as-built network; maintain a separately approved target design.

FigureUseWhat must be verified
16 — segmentation modelsOrganize zones, conduits and DMZ boundariesActual trust boundaries and enforcement; levels alone do not define permissions
17 / 18 — DCS and secured DCSMap local plant control, operations, engineering and enterprise interfacesActual switches/routes, applications, segmentation, redundancy and access
19 — DCS with IIoTAdd edge/platform connections only where presentGateway direction, broker/API behavior, cloud dependencies and control capability

NIST SP 800-82 Rev. 3, Figures 16–21 and §5.2.3

Plain lines mean connectivity, not data direction or access approval. On the site version, label every interface, subnet/VLAN, device ID, route, firewall/conduit ID, redundant link and capture point. Show each management path, dual-homed device and blind spot. Do not place an assumed IP address, port or device on the as-built drawing.

3. Identify assets and capture their attributes

Start with engineering records, equipment lists, network configurations, existing monitoring and site validation. Reconcile these sources; passive discovery alone does not reveal every disconnected, serial, silent or unmonitored asset. Any additional probing requires site-specific qualification and authorization.

CISA’s joint inventory guidance identifies core fields such as role, criticality, hostname, addresses, location, manufacturer/model, protocols, ports/services, logging and accounts. The expanded schema below adds SOC operational requirements; it is not a verbatim CISA field list. CISA and partners — OT Asset Inventory Guidance, Appendix A

Attribute groupFields to captureSOC purpose
Identity and provenanceOrganization ID; site ID; stable asset ID; equipment tag; hostname; serial/asset number; source of information; confidence; last verification; validatorPrevent incorrect joins; track uncertainty and ownership
Physical/process locationPlant; area; unit; production line; cabinet/rack; remote-station location; process servedIdentify operational consequences and local responder
Role and technologyPLC/RTU/DCS/HMI/SIS/drive/server/network device; vendor; model; firmware; OS; engineering application/version; installed modulesSelect supported telemetry and applicable detections
Network identityAll interfaces; IP/subnet; MAC where applicable; VLAN; security zone; switch/port; gateway; NAT mappings; serial/unit address; wireless/cellular linksResolve traffic correctly, including multi-homed and non-IP assets
CommunicationsRequired peers; initiator; protocols; transport/ports; industrial functions; authentication/encryption; flow IDsDistinguish permitted communications from deviations
Ownership and supportOperational owner; control engineer; network owner; OEM/integrator; support entitlement; escalation contacts and alternatesReach qualified staff and establish response authority
Criticality and dependenciesSafety/environment/production impact; dependent equipment/services; redundancy; failover; operational availability limitsPrioritize incidents and assess containment impact
Identity and accessApproved users/roles; service-account references; vendor access route; privileged access method; local/shared accounts; MFA enforcement pointInterpret sessions and privileged actions; store references, not passwords
Telemetry and visibilityNative audit capability; enabled events; collector/sensor IDs; monitored interface; source IDs; parser; time source; clock offset; gapsEstablish what evidence can support a conclusion
Configuration and lifecycleApproved configuration/program reference; backup location; restoration validation date; lifecycle/support status; change record; approved maintenance windowValidate changes and recovery readiness
Response constraintsPermitted evidence collection; who authorizes isolation/restart; safe-state prerequisites; OEM restrictions; restoration dependenciesPrevent an investigation from disrupting production

Initial acceptance: critical in-scope assets have a stable ID, process role, owner, location, zone, address/interface information, criticality, known dependencies and visibility status. Unknown fields are explicitly marked with an owner and resolution date. An IP address is an attribute, not the permanent asset identity.

4. How commands and measurements communicate

Industrial communication must distinguish an operator request, controller decision, actuator command, measured feedback and historical record. The example below explains those relationships without assigning site-specific tags, process limits or protocols.

The sensor-to-historian arrow represents information lineage, not a required direct network session. The actual acquisition route may pass through the controller, SCADA, an OPC server or another approved source. Physical effect arrows do not represent Ethernet connections. This drawing does not establish a safety function.

StepWhat may happenWhat evidence can establish
1 — requestOperator asks the HMI to change a setpoint or equipment stateHMI/application audit can identify a requested action and user where logged
2 — transmissionHMI sends a protocol request to the controllerSupported protocol or application records can establish the operation attempted
3 — evaluationController evaluates mode, logic, permissions and interlocksAvailable controller records or engineering interpretation establish acceptance/rejection
4 — outputController issues an actuator command if applicableCommand tag/output state records the commanded state
5 — feedbackEquipment response and process measurements are observedIndependent feedback and quality-checked measurements support an effect claim
6 — recordSelected observations are storedHistorian timestamps, quality and sampling define what the record can support

A request is not acceptance; acceptance is not actuator movement; actuator movement is not proof of the predicted process outcome. Retain evidence for each link separately.

5. Define the permitted flows

The following is a document convention, consistent with documenting connectivity and required information flows; it is not claimed to be an official NIST/CISA arrow notation. NCSC’s joint guidance calls for documented connectivity and DFDs. NCSC and partners — Document connectivity within your OT system

Symbol/useMeaningRequired annotation
Plain line A — B on topology viewPhysical or logical connectivity; no claim about authorization or payload directionInterface/link type, zone boundary and enforcement device
Solid arrow A → B on operational DFDNamed application request, command or data payload travels from A to BFlow ID, purpose and operation; initiator is separately recorded
Separate arrows A → B and B → ARequest/response or different payloads in opposite directionsLabel each direction; do not use a vague bidirectional arrow
Dashed arrow on telemetry viewSecurity-event export, mirrored traffic or reference-data feedLabel which of these it is; capture does not imply control access
Zone box / boundary labelTrust or operational boundaryZone ID and enforcement reference; show as-built versus proposed
One-way arrowDirection of the illustrated logical flow onlyA hardware-enforced one-way path requires an explicit diode/gateway symbol and evidence

For an HMI read, show HMI → PLC: read request and PLC → HMI: measurement response. The HMI initiates the session even though the measurement travels back. TCP acknowledgements are normally omitted from an application DFD. For subscriptions, record setup direction and subsequent notification direction separately.

Operational data-flow diagram — commands and measurements

This DFD illustrates client-initiated acquisition. If an installed source pushes data instead, update the direction and session-initiator record. Payload direction is not necessarily session-initiation direction. A one-way arrow is not evidence of a data diode.

Register fieldRequired site value
IdentityFlow ID; source/destination stable asset IDs; source/destination zones; diagram revision
DirectionSession initiator; request direction; payload/response direction; whether push, polling or subscription
Transport and semanticsProtocol; actual configured port or serial address; operation; relevant tag/register/node/topic; encryption/authentication
Purpose and dependencyBusiness/process purpose; upstream/downstream dependency; latency and availability constraints
AuthorizationApproved source/user/service role; targets; operations; mode; time window; exception expiry; approving owner
EnforcementFirewall/conduit/gateway and policy references; intended versus actually enforced restrictions
EvidenceLogging source; sensor visibility; observed outcome; sample reference; missing fields
LifecycleVerified present/absent/unknown; validation date; reviewer; next review; change record

OP01–OP06 are document example identifiers, not plant allowlist entries. Actual protocols, ports, addresses and approvals remain to be confirmed. Connectivity documentation guidance.

6. Where to collect SIEM evidence

Evidence sourceEvents/context to collectQualification requirement
Firewalls, routers, VPN and remote accessAllowed/denied sessions, initiator, translated addresses, authentication, configuration changesConfirm field semantics, site attribution, routing visibility and retention
Passive OT sensorsConnection records, supported industrial operations, alerts and capture healthValidate mirror/TAP coverage, loss, throughput, protocol support and encrypted blind spots
Engineering/operations endpointsProcess creation, logon, privileged activity and supported endpoint detectionsOEM/site-qualified collection; confirm event policy and application identity
SCADA/HMI/OPC and engineering applicationsOperator actions, changes, sessions, alarms and audit eventsDemonstrate actual audit granularity and distinguish request, acceptance and result
PLC/RTU/DCS/SISAvailable configuration, mode, diagnostic and audit eventsDevice-specific capability; approved retrieval; no assumed endpoint-agent support
Historian and process recordsSelected tags, mode, command/feedback, quality and timestampsDocument sampling/compression; validate retrieval without creating process load
Identity, time, backup and infrastructureAccess, privileged changes, time drift, backup/restore and infrastructure failuresValidate operational dependencies and supported collection
SIEM and collection infrastructureHeartbeats, queue depth, ingestion delay, parser failures, dropped events and storage statusExercise interruption/buffering and restoration; detect monitoring loss

Collection Management Framework: investigation question → source/location → event/fields → access owner → approved retrieval method → retention → timestamp uncertainty → sample/retrieval evidence → known gap/fallback. A configured connector is not evidence of readiness until a representative event is retrieved successfully.

Separate sensor capture interfaces from management. Keep security-management access scoped to designated systems, with no general routing bridge into control cells. Transport protection, data residency and read access must match organization requirements.

Observation locationPotential evidenceCoverage question
Enterprise / DMZ / OT boundaryFirewall and access sessions, denied traffic and exported data pathsAre both legitimate and unapproved cross-boundary paths visible, including NAT?
Production-cell switch/TAPLocal HMI, controller and engineering exchangesDoes the mirror include intra-cell traffic and both directions without significant loss?
Engineering workstationApplication execution, user/session, project and endpoint recordsIs supported process/audit collection enabled and validated?
Remote access entry and targetGateway authentication, MFA, broker session and target logon/auditCan the same identity/session be traced through address translation and shared hosts?
Remote station / radio gatewayCommunications diagnostics, RTU events and observable network sessionsWhich serial/radio paths cannot be observed by the IP sensor?
IIoT gateway / platformConnection, broker/API, identity and device-management recordsAre command channels and cloud access observable, or only outbound telemetry?
Historian / control-room recordsValues, modes, quality, operator observations and alarmsAre sampling, clock offsets and independent feedback adequate for the investigation?

7. Overlay security evidence collection

Dashed arrows mean evidence/reference transfer in this view; they are not process-control paths. A DMZ relay may be required by the approved site design and should be explicitly inserted where deployed. Show administrative access separately from telemetry transport. Detection may run before or after indexing depending on the actual platform.

  • For each TEL flow, record source, collector, transport, parser, site/asset identifiers, timestamp behavior, latency, retention, owner and failure handling.
  • Trace an existing representative event from source to normalized record and alert. Record exactly which fields were lost, enriched or inferred.
  • Monitor sensor/collector health, queue growth, parser failures and data delay. Silence may indicate a collection failure rather than an absence of activity.
  • Treat process data as context requiring quality and time validation. Do not label a sensor signature as a confirmed write if the underlying record cannot distinguish reads and writes.

NIST SP 1800-23, Volume B — monitoring architecture

8. Supporting registers you need

RegisterMinimum contentsAcceptance evidence
Asset registerStable identity, role, attributes, process owner, criticality, location/zone, provenance and verification stateCritical assets reconciled with engineering and network records
Communication registerDirectional flows, purpose, initiator, authorization, enforcement and dependenciesEvery operational DFD flow linked to a reviewed record
Tag / object dictionaryMeaning, address/object, units/scaling, type, command/feedback/measurement, quality and update rateControl engineer validates selected process interpretations
Baseline registerObserved behavior and separately approved behavior by operating mode; excluded/unobserved modesOperational review, version and representative coverage recorded
Access / change registerUsers/roles, access routes, approved engineering sources, activity/target scope, window and emergency processAuthorization lookup has owner, freshness and exception expiry
Collection Management FrameworkQuestion, source, fields, location, retention, retrieval owner/method, clock uncertainty and gapsRepresentative evidence retrieved through an approved path
Detection / validation registerHypothesis, prerequisites, query/version, positive/negative tests, limitations, runbook and response authorityEvidence-supported outcomes and production qualification recorded
External and alternative path registerRemote, cellular, wireless, dual-homed, temporary and removable-media pathsOwner, physical/logical endpoint, authorization and monitoring gap recorded

Assign a record owner and review trigger to every register. Plant changes must update diagrams, inventory, approvals, baselines and detection dependencies together.

9. Record connections that can bypass the main boundary

These paths may be legitimate, unauthorized or absent. Inventory them explicitly and verify their routing and operating purpose; do not assume they are all bypasses or malicious.

Potential pathWhat to establishPotential evidence
Vendor cellular routers or modemsOwner, SIM/carrier, remote endpoint, connected equipment, routing, access approval and disable procedureRouter/VPN logs, carrier records where available, physical inspection
Dual-homed engineering laptopsAll wired/wireless interfaces, VPN routes, bridging/forwarding state, approved useEndpoint network configuration, interface events, switch/AP/VPN records
Temporary maintenance connectionsWho connects what, where, for how long, under which work order; removal confirmationAccess/change records, switch-port events, endpoint/engineering audit
Wireless bridges and access pointsBridge endpoints, authentication, associated devices, zone extension and RF coverageAP/controller audit, authentication and network records
Serial-to-Ethernet gatewaysSerial device/unit mapping, network peers, supported operations and management routeGateway configuration/logs, serial diagnostics and observable IP sessions
Remote-site WAN linksCarrier, tunnels, alternate/failover paths, station routes and control authorityWAN/VPN/firewall records, communications and SCADA diagnostics
Cloud-connected equipment gatewaysOutbound destinations, inbound command capability, broker identity, vendor access and dependenciesGateway, API/broker, platform audit and firewall/DNS records
USB media and portable engineering projectsMedia ownership, transfer/work order, project provenance, inspection policy and destinationSupported device-control/endpoint events, project audit and chain-of-custody records

USB and portable projects are data-transfer paths, not network sessions. A network-only diagram and passive sensor cannot establish their full use.

10. Detections with remote access into OT

Remote access requires evidence from the entry point through the target and, where relevant, the engineering action. No particular VPN, PAM, identity provider, endpoint agent or logging product is assumed installed.

The RA arrows illustrate separately scoped access/action stages. A gateway is not evidence that MFA, approval, recording or segmentation is actually enforced. Validate those controls independently. Correlate with session IDs, identities, timestamps, gateway/NAT mapping and target records; do not infer a user solely from controller traffic.

Detection hypothesisMinimum evidence and contextInvestigation and interpretation
Remote access outside an approved windowAccess start/continuation, site/user/target, applicable authorization and approval-feed healthDifferentiate no matching approval from unavailable data; review emergency access
Remote access to an unapproved OT targetGateway/broker destination plus approved target scope and address mappingConfirm target identity and whether connection succeeded; establish subsequent activity
Remote access through a bypass pathObserved route or target logon plus approved access-path inventoryExclude legitimate alternate/failover routes; identify endpoint owner and authorization
New remote identity or deviceReliable identity/device record plus maintained baselineFirst-seen is a review signal, not proof of compromise; validate onboarding and device evidence
Repeated authentication failure followed by successAuthentication records with consistent identity/session context and timestampsCheck user error, stale credentials and service retries; successful login alone does not prove abuse
Remote session followed by engineering software executionGateway/target session plus endpoint process records and application inventoryValidate the session-to-process association, parent process and approved diagnostics
Remote session followed by unapproved controller changeAccess chain plus engineering/controller action evidence and change scopeDistinguish attempted, rejected and accepted operations; validate device semantics
Remote session followed by process deviationSupported action record plus related tags, mode, quality and time alignmentKeep correlation separate from causation; examine process faults and authorized intervention
Remote-access control or telemetry changesGateway/PAM/identity configuration audit and source healthVerify approved changes; establish whether access controls or evidence collection were affected

For every analytic, define fields, grouping keys, rule windows, severity rationale, maintenance handling, missing-data behavior, deduplication and validation cases from the actual environment. No numeric threshold is supplied without site evidence.

When an event requires intervention, the SOC provides evidence and proposed options to the designated operational authority. Session termination, account restriction or workstation isolation must follow the approved plant response matrix.

11. Other initial detections

Initial analyticRequired evidence/contextRelease gate
Unapproved OT outbound connectionAsset/zone mapping; connection initiator and outcome; approved peers/purposesAllowed, blocked, unapproved and unknown-zone cases are correctly distinguished
Engineering software outside authorizationEndpoint process event; application inventory; matching site/user/asset/activity windowApproved diagnostics and stale approval feeds handled; long-running application limitation documented
Unauthorized industrial writeDecoded operation or application audit; source/target mapping; approved writersRead versus write supported; attempted/rejected/accepted distinguished where possible
Configuration changeEngineering/controller evidence; approved project/configuration reference and change scopeActual evidence supports change claim; authorized maintenance included in testing
Engineering action with process deviationRelevant action plus mapped process measurements, mode and qualityTime and relationship validated; equipment fault/operator alternatives considered
Monitoring lossExpected reporting or heartbeat, collection status, maintenance scheduleLoss distinguished from naturally silent assets and planned maintenance

Use controlled offline replay and approved non-disruptive validation; move to production shadow monitoring before operational acceptance. Record source coverage, representative operating modes, alert workload, missed-test cases and known limitations. Do not report scripted-test accuracy as a production detection rate.

Each analytic needs an owner, version, evidence prerequisites, query, severity rationale, exceptions with expiry, regression tests, analyst runbook and approved response route. Do not suppress unauthorized engineering actions solely because no process effect is observed.

12. Process context and baseline requirements

Required recordContentsValidation owner
Process dependency mapAsset → equipment → process unit → production/safety/environmental consequence; upstream/downstream dependenciesProcess and control engineering
Tag and object dictionaryTag/register/node/topic; device; units/scaling; data type; command vs feedback vs measurement; access rights; quality; update rateControl engineering
Operating-mode baselineStartup, steady operation, shutdown, batch/recipe phases, cleaning, maintenance and failover; representative observations and unobserved modesPlant operations
Engineering-change baselineAuthorized workstations/users, controller project/program references, permitted maintenance, emergency changes and expiryControl engineering + change owner
Network baselineApproved peers/operations plus separately recorded observed patterns; polling, volumes, errors and occasional legitimate flowsNetwork/security engineer with plant validation

Keep approved engineering limits separate from observed statistical ranges. Confirm timestamp quality, historian sampling/compression and clock uncertainty before inferring event order. Never automatically promote unexplained activity into the approved baseline.

13. SIEM engineering and capacity

  • Define a normalized field contract: organization/site, stable asset ID, event source, event time, ingest time, source/destination, action, outcome, identity/session and evidence reference; specify required fields per source.
  • Preserve raw records and source identifiers. Document parsing, time conversion and enrichment versions so analysts can trace conclusions back to originals.
  • Measure average and peak event/byte rates, burst duration, network capacity and ingest delay. Size buffering from measured peak throughput × required outage tolerance, with an explicit margin.
  • Select searchable retention, archive retention, packet retention and historian retrieval windows based on investigation needs and organization requirements. Do not apply one duration to every source.
  • Enforce organization isolation, scoped analyst access, administrative auditing, credential management and approved data-export paths.
  • Specify recovery objectives and test backup/recovery of collectors, configuration, reference tables and detection content. Loss of the SOC must not prevent local process control.

14. OT incident response and decision authority

ActivitySOC responsibilityPlant/site responsibility
Triage and investigationPreserve source references, construct timeline, identify uncertainty and possible affected assetsConfirm operating mode, maintenance activity and local observations
Evidence retrievalUse pre-agreed collection methods; preserve originals and custody; record clocks and collection impactProvide approved access, engineering interpretation and OEM coordination
ContainmentRecommend scoped options and operational dependencies; execute only within explicit authorityAuthorize process-affecting action; establish safe state and fallback with engineering
RecoverySupport validation, monitoring and incident documentationAuthorize restoration and confirm process/control/safety readiness with qualified personnel
CommunicationsMaintain incident record, update cadence and shift handoverMaintain reachable control-room lead, incident commander, alternates and external reporting owner

Define response authority for account restriction, vendor-session termination, workstation isolation, firewall changes, controller actions and restoration individually. Silence from a plant approver is not authorization. An incident bridge must have a fallback communication channel.

Exercise both SOC-led and control-room-led intake, approved-maintenance lookalikes, unavailable approvers, missing telemetry and independent recovery evidence. A return to normal dashboards alone is not sufficient recovery verification.

15. People, governance and ongoing operations

Role/capabilityResponsibility
SOC analystsContinuous triage under agreed coverage, evidence-led escalation and case handling
OT investigation/detection specialistsIndustrial protocol interpretation, use-case engineering, hunting and site-context maintenance
OT architect / collection engineerSite design, sensor placement, integrations, access boundaries and collection health
Organization plant operationsOperational authority, current process state and local incident coordination
Organization control/process engineeringTag and logic interpretation, change approval, safe action and recovery validation
Organization IT/network and OEM/integratorSupporting infrastructure, network changes and product-specific support
Service ownerScope, SLAs, review cadence, gap acceptance and capacity management

Define specialist on-call coverage separately from SOC intake hours. SLAs should distinguish acknowledgement, investigation, notification, specialist engagement and organization-authorized action. Production restoration depends on plant and OEM decisions and should not be promised as a generic SOC resolution time.

Review critical-asset coverage, monitored-flow coverage, data latency/quality, evidence retrieval, alert workload, exceptions and accepted blind spots. Use a validated denominator before publishing coverage percentages. Update asset records, diagrams, baselines and rules after approved changes and incidents.

16. Deployment logistics and staged acceptance

GateWork and deliverableAcceptance evidence
G1 — Scope and discoveryService scope; roles; existing records; site survey; critical asset inventorySOC and plant owners validate scope, ownership and unknowns
G2 — Architecture and process contextAs-built topology; operational DFD; communication matrix; process/tag referencesRepresentative paths traced; critical process dependencies validated
G3 — Collection designSensor/collector design; source matrix; transport, capacity and retention planSource samples and supported retrieval methods; gaps assigned to owners
G4 — Deployment readinessSite induction/access; rack/power/environment; cabling/optics; mirror/TAP plan; IPs; firewall changes; maintenance window; rollback; spares/RMAApproved method of procedure, OEM restrictions and change authorization
G5 — Technical commissioningCollectors, parsers, clocks, reference tables and telemetry healthRaw event traced to case; buffering/recovery and tenant isolation verified
G6 — Operational qualificationMode-aware baseline; initial rules; shadow monitoring; escalation exerciseExpected test outcomes, agreed alert workload and successful control-room handoff
G7 — Service acceptanceRunbooks, response authority, SLAs, support handover, limitations and backlogAsset owner signs agreed coverage and explicitly accepts remaining gaps

Sequence work around actual plant access, procurement and maintenance windows. Do not declare full monitoring coverage merely because hardware is installed or logs appear in a dashboard.
